Doesn't bv_decide trust the compiler?
It trusts the compiler in the sense that it trusts that it was itself compiled correctly. You cannot use it to do tricks like native_decide etc.

Assuming the above question is addressed to Alex, I'll move to the next question:

Lastly, is it open to contributions?
Actually I would argue that for computational purposes, adjacency ought to be explicitly algorithmic : computed by looking up the adj list of one of the vertices.

(answering Yakov's first because it's the easiest): yes, I think quite easily so. There's verified algorithms for testing various inclusions, like testing subgraph/induced subgraph/homomorphism/minor/subdivision. (I forgot to mention this in my initial post!)

Common substructure could be built, I think, as aetaprogram that says "compute me a new graph H, together with embeddings f1: G1 -> H and f2: G2 -> H, and a proof term that H is maximal for this". It would be a natural addition.

Shreyas Srinivas said:

Actually I would argue that for computational purposes, adjacency ought to be explicitly algorithmic : computed by looking up the adj list of one of the vertices.

I wanted adjacency to be the main "primitive" operation, and arguably that is one of the main ones that algorithms need. Materializing a list of all neighbors for an adjacency query could be quite expensive. It also seemed most natural in how it composed with most graph operations: join, product, complement, etc.

There's certainly room for some improved performance if you give CGraph an adjList : V -> List V (or Multiset V) field, together with axioms that is compatible with adj; and a default constructor to build one from the other. This felt lower priority to me as there's lots of room for other performance improvements first though.

(Of note: Mathlib's existing FinEnum instances are very very slow for actual computation and I overrode them with my own. No shade to Mathlib, it's optimized for proofs of course.)

One reason was that I wanted only simple was that I wanted a mostly easy correspondence with Mathlib's SimpleGraph type. There are myriad extensions like loops, multi edges, directed edges, hypergraphs, and coloring edges and vertices. Any of these would be welcome as a PR for a new type, but I think CGraph shouldn't embrace this (with probably the sole e exception of self loops): I want it to mostly match what is most standard in graph theory literature, and plenty of operations don't have a standard definition.

It would also significantly complicate many of the algorithms, and there's a great deal of literature on smart efficient algorithms that only deal with the undirected simple case. I'm happy to see algorithms extended, but that also increasingly becomes "new research math".

Shreyas Srinivas said:

I am proposing lists mostly because that directly gives us multigraphs. So writing a constructor to CGraph would be impossible without losing structure. But we could say that the constructor captures the underlying simple graph topology of the multigraph.

Here's a wacky idea: if we have vertex and edge labels (which would be an extension to CGraph I would be fine with, I think), then we can talk about a simple graph with Nat labels on vertices and PNat labels on edges. The label on a vertex can be interpreted as a statement about how many self-loops there are, while the label on an edge counts how many copies of the edge there are. (Alternately, if you hate dealing with PNat -- a reasonable reaction -- we can use Nat labels on the edge and it counts "how many extra copies there are".)

This creates a reasonably natural isomorphism now between list-of-edge multigraphs, and labelled graphs.

I think this might also enable some kind of sensible compatibility with other predicates for different label types. Now if you talk about one labelled graph being an induced subgraph of another, you're saying that all induced edges must be present, and the edge labels must match, so this gives the natural notion of induced subgraph for the multigraph as well.

What about for (non-induced) subgraph? Now the requirement is that the labels are monotone: the label on a vertex or edge of H must be at most the label on the corresponding vertex or edge of G. This would be the case for Nat labels. For "color" labels, the relation is instead the bottom preorder, where no distinct colors are less than or equal each other.

I haven't thought fully through what happens with minors or quotients (I'm not sure if there is a super standard notion, for labelled graphs or multigraphs), but this could be an interesting path towards building something that serves both needs in one go! What do you think?

I like the explicit quotienting up to iso. That is something I always liked the idea of. However, I never tried seriously because for each new def on labelled graph, I would need to prove that it is invariant under Iso and define the same notion on the quotient again. I am very curious to know how @[toIsoGraph] works.

I have been recently thinking about and trying to write an exact specification for a tactic I call irw, rw under not equality but isomorphism. With a categorical hat on, each object naturally have a notion of iso. So perhaps with a tag system, a tactic could memorize what notion of iso is appropriate for an object and what natural functions are, then it could recognize a composition of natural functions as natural and, given isomorphism, rw the statement to appropriate statement for the isomorphic object.

I am very curious to know how @[toIsoGraph] works.

Thanks! The idea is that you define the quantity once for the graph (not up to isomorphism), and then you prove the theorem that it's an isomorphism invariant: a theorem of the shape (h : G ≃g H) : f G = f H. When you tag this theorem with @[toIsoGraph], then it creates the definition on the quotient type, using the appropriate lift.

It handles other shapes, too. For instance, operations like lineGraph map graphs to graphs, and so you prove that (h : G ≃g H) : lineGraph G ≃g lineGraph H - so there's an isomorphism in the conclusion. This lifts to defining a lineGraph function from IsoGraph to IsoGraph. In general, it can handle arbitrary "arity" functions, and it translates any ismorphisms between graphs into equalities on IsoGraphs.

This also works for things like predicates -- so, if you show that "is a minor of" is an isomorphism invariant in both arguments, then you get the corresponding predicate defined on IsoGraphs.

Theorems (well, technically, defs, because isomorphisms carry data) like compl (cycle 5) ≃g cycle 5 get lifted to theorems like compl (IsoGraph.cycle 5) = IsoGraph.cycle 5. By writing @[toIsoGraph simp], the resulting theorem becomes a simp lemma. This way we can aggregate a bunch of rewriting to put many graphs in a "canonical" description.

It also keeps a tag system internally (which you can query) of which definitions match up where, which theorems match up where, and so on, in case you want to override a default name; this dictionary is used in constructing more complicated things. (Like, the compl in the above example refers to two different operations -- one for graphs, one for isographs -- and so it needs that dictionary to produce the correct final statement.)
